scenarios.title: EOL conversion: obligation does not see tree bytes
scenarios.expected: the obligation must see the bytes of the verified tree (the Git blob), or the run must be refused as unfaithful
scenarios.observed: PASSED: the obligation asserted CRLF and succeeded, while the tree blob for payload.txt is LF (11 bytes: 'line1\nline2'); the receipt names the tree whose blob was never tested. The checkout conversion is driven by a committed .gitattributes (`*.txt text eol=crlf`).
scenarios.notes: P1: this is the content-fidelity counterpart of the P0-1 type-fidelity fix. `verify_checkout_fidelity` checks presence and file type, not that the bytes on disk equal the blob. `doctor` warns that eol/filter rules can change bytes (only when .gitattributes is present), so the limitation is partly disclosed, but the headline claim 'the receipt names the exact Git tree that was checked' is not literally true for converted files.

scenarios.title: Journal symlink -> write outside the workspace
scenarios.expected: Flow must not follow a symlinked `.flow/journal.jsonl` to write outside its workspace
scenarios.observed: PUBLISHED appended 514 bytes of journal records to 'outside-victim.txt' OUTSIDE the repository (14 -> 528 bytes, sha256 1fc87ad022bb -> 7241e0afe7df)
scenarios.notes: P0: `.flow` state paths are used without checking that they are regular files inside the workspace. An absolute symlink planted in `.flow` (or shipped by a cloned repository on a symlink-capable host, see FIL-clone-*) turns `flow publish` into an arbitrary-file append. The report's own boundary is violated: a user file outside the repository changed.

scenarios.title: Receipts symlink -> write outside the workspace
scenarios.expected: Flow must not follow a symlinked `.flow/receipts` to write outside its workspace
scenarios.observed: run exited 0 and wrote receipt ['5da9bb037560f218b886f3b5bd3bf89d312259aa.json'] into 'outside-receipts' OUTSIDE the repository
scenarios.notes: P0: same unchecked-state-path class as the journal symlink. `save_receipt` creates the directory (following a link) and renames a temp file into it. A repository can ship `.flow/receipts` as a symlink (see FIL-clone-receipts), so this is reachable from a cloned candidate, not only from a local prank.

scenarios.title: Logs junction -> write outside `.flow` (inside repo)
scenarios.expected: logs must stay under `.flow`, not be redirected into the user's source tree
scenarios.observed: run wrote ['green.stderr.log', 'green.stdout.log'] into the junction target `src/`; only the repository boundary is checked, not the `.flow` boundary
scenarios.notes: P2: canonical_within(root) is enforced for the log directory, so an outside-the-repository redirect is refused, but a junction to another directory *inside* the repository is accepted and user source files appear there. Requires a pre-existing link; low impact, recorded for completeness.

scenarios.title: Cloned repo ships a receipts symlink
scenarios.expected: a cloned repository must not be able to redirect Flow's receipt write outside the checkout
scenarios.observed: clone materialised `.flow/receipts` as a symlink; `flow run` wrote ['baf41f8b26ef7f8cec53bdecdfde3c1b986a38fa.json'] into 'clone-receipts-out' outside the clone
scenarios.notes: P0: supply-chain variant of FIL-state-receipts. The link is committed in the candidate tree; the victim only runs the documented workflow (`flow run`). Reproduced on hosts where Git materialises symlinks (Linux, macOS, Windows with Developer Mode); the default Windows clone on this host materialises a plain file and the fidelity check refuses (FIL-clone-default).

scenarios.title: Cloned repo ships a journal symlink
scenarios.expected: a cloned repository must not be able to redirect Flow's journal append outside the checkout
scenarios.observed: clone materialised `.flow/journal.jsonl` as a symlink; `flow publish` appended 514 bytes of journal to a file OUTSIDE the clone (16 -> 530 bytes)
scenarios.notes: P0: supply-chain variant of FIL-state-journal. A candidate tree that tracks `.flow/journal.jsonl` as a symlink makes the victim's ordinary `flow publish` append to an attacker-chosen file. Absolute symlink targets survive clone verbatim.

scenarios.title: Cloned repo ships a journal symlink (default clone)
scenarios.expected: on a host where Git cannot materialise the symlink, the fidelity check refuses the tree instead of certifying it
scenarios.observed: clone wrote a regular file; run refused UNSUPPORTED_CHECKOUT
scenarios.notes: This is the protection that exists today: on this host `core.symlinks=false` by default, so a committed symlink becomes a plain file and `verify_checkout_fidelity` refuses. It does not help on symlink-capable hosts (Linux/macOS/Developer Mode), see FIL-clone-receipts.

scenarios.title: Cloned repo ships `.flow/config.json`
scenarios.expected: `flow run` must not execute a program supplied by the repository without saying so
scenarios.observed: the cloned repo's `.flow/config.json` was used by `flow run` and its obligation executed (config-executed.txt written); run status=PASSED
scenarios.notes: P1: documented residual in the hardening report §8 ('a repository can ship .flow/config.json and have it used without flow init'), but the operational consequence - a cloned candidate executes arbitrary commands under the documented `flow run` workflow - is not surfaced at run time and contradicts the intent of verifying an untrusted candidate. `doctor` does not warn that the active policy came from the repository.

scenarios.title: post-checkout hook: what runs today
scenarios.expected: documented: Flow dispatches no hook of its own, but `git worktree add` runs a `post-checkout` hook; it executes with cwd = the scratch checkout and user files are untouched
scenarios.notes: Observed behaviour today, matching `doctor`'s non-guarantee wording. This is the HOOK-GITDIR-19 boundary: a hook can reach the shared git directory; Flow refuses only when the hook aborts Git, not when it writes.

scenarios.title: FLOW_TEST_CRASH in the shipped binary
scenarios.expected: a test-only crash switch is honoured unconditionally by the shipped binary and exits 89, outside the documented exit-code contract (0/1/2)
scenarios.observed: FLOW_TEST_CRASH=after-intent -> exit 89; after-ref -> exit 89; unrecognised value -> exit 1
scenarios.notes: P2: observed while testing durability. The hook is not compiled out and not gated by an opt-in flag; it can abort a publication between intent and CAS (or after CAS) in any environment where the variable is set. Impact is limited to denial/forced recovery, but it is a test backdoor in a production binary and exit 89 is outside the documented contract.

scenarios.title: Unknown options / missing option values
scenarios.expected: unknown options and options missing their value must be usage errors (exit 2), never a live database- or ref-mutating action
scenarios.observed: `publish --dry-run` -> PUBLISHED (ref moved: True); `publish --ref` with no value -> PUBLISHED (ref moved: True); `run --obligation` with no value -> FAILED (both obligations executed: True)
scenarios.notes: P1: the argv parser ignores every token it does not know and treats a flag without its value as absent. An operator asking for a dry run publishes; a truncated `--ref` publishes to the current branch; a truncated `--obligation` runs the whole policy (a red required obligation makes it FAILED here, proving both ran). The documented usage-error exit code (2) is never used for these cases.

scenarios.title: Re-sealed forged receipt
scenarios.expected: a receipt must not be forgeable by a writer who can also edit and re-seal the file
scenarios.observed: PUBLISHED a commit for a tree whose required obligation was FAILED: status and obligation entries edited, integrity digest recomputed (0bc37d63ec15...)
scenarios.notes: P2: exactly the documented honest boundary ('no cryptographic protection of a receipt: anyone who can write .flow/receipts can forge one'). Reproduced empirically so the report's claim is measured, not assumed. Severity P2, not P0: the limitation is stated in `doctor` and in the hardening report; only a signature could close it. The casual edit (no re-seal) is refused with RECEIPT_INTEGRITY (IDN-11).

scenarios.title: Log files deleted after the run

scenarios.observed: PUBLISHED with all 2 log files deleted; publish output reports receipt_logs=2
scenarios.notes: P3 observation: not a gate breach (the receipt's own content is intact and still binds tree+policy), but `receipt_logs` in the publish output reads as if the logs were present. The receipt lists paths; nothing verifies they exist.

scenarios.title: Tampered receipt displayed by status/explain
scenarios.expected: `status` and `explain` must not present a receipt whose integrity digest no longer matches
scenarios.observed: status reports latest_receipt.status=PASSED from a receipt that publish refuses with RECEIPT_INTEGRITY; explain echoes the same tampered receipt
scenarios.notes: P2: the publication gate holds (publish refuses), but the human-facing report shows a false green. An operator checking `flow status` sees PASSED for an edited receipt.

scenarios.title: Doctor honesty and exit code
scenarios.expected: `doctor` must fail the process (or at least not exit 0) when its own journal check is FAILED, and its disclosures must match the code
scenarios.observed: journal check FAILED, overall=FAILED, but exit=0; forge disclosed=True, eol/filter in static non_guarantees=False (only the conditional `gitattributes` check mentions it)
scenarios.notes: P2: `doctor` exits 0 because its status is REPORT (the documented code for 'a report was printed'), so a CI job checking only the exit code treats a corrupt journal as success. The forgery boundary is disclosed and matches PRF-forge-receipt; the checkout byte-conversion limit is disclosed only when `.gitattributes` is present, which is a weaker promise than the report implies.

scenarios.title: `explain --tree` path traversal
scenarios.expected: `explain --tree` must validate the tree argument, not read an arbitrary JSON file by path traversal or absolute path
scenarios.observed: explain --tree 'C:\\Users\\barat\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\flow-mvp-qa-qfgi0q8d\\PRF-06\\outside-secret' returned the outside file content {"secret": "CANARY-FAKE-SECRET-001"}; traversal '../../../outside-secret' returned {"secret": "CANARY-FAKE-SECRET-001"}
scenarios.notes: P2: `receipt_path` joins the unvalidated `--tree` value to `.flow/receipts/<value>.json`; an absolute path replaces the base. Read-only (no write), but it is the PATH-08 class the project claims to validate, and it can echo any readable JSON file.

scenarios.title: Two concurrent runs
scenarios.expected: two concurrent runs must not corrupt the receipt or report a false PASSED
scenarios.observed: passed=1 failed=1 receipts=['aaca6f6b8a7a9c0aa154e87614ed60b93bf38750.json'] errors=['git ["write-tree"] failed (128): fatal: Unable to create \'C:']
scenarios.notes: Concurrent runs are not serialised (only publish/reconcile take the advisory lock). The losing process fails loudly with a typed ERROR such as a Git index.lock collision; a retry succeeds. No corruption and no false PASSED was observed; the single complete receipt is well formed.
